body:
`case_study:yes-bank-2020` | 2020-03-05 | tickers: YESBANK | confidence: verified

Yes Bank peaked near Rs 393-404 in Aug 2018 and hit ~Rs 5.6 on 6 Mar 2020 (-98%) after RBI superseded the board and imposed a moratorium (withdrawals capped at Rs 50,000) on 5 Mar 2020. An SBI-led consortium recapitalised it at Rs 10/share; Rs 8,415 cr of AT1 bonds were written off; ~75% of existing shares were locked in for 3 years. Visible flags well before: (1) RBI-assessed NPA divergence: ~Rs 4,177 cr in FY16 and ~Rs 6,355 cr in FY17 (reported NPAs were a fraction of RBI's); (2) loan book growing 30-35%/yr with corporate concentration in stressed groups (ADAG, Essel, DHFL, IL&FS, Cox & Kings, Jet, CG Power); (3) low CASA and dependence on bulk/high-cost deposits; (4) Sep 2018 RBI refused to extend founder Rana Kapoor's term -- a regulator vote of no confidence; (5) promoter shares pledged and sold by lenders; (6) independent director exit in Jan 2019; GNPA jumped from 1.3% (FY18) to 3.2% (FY19) to 7.4% (Sep 2019). Who spotted it: RBI inspections (divergence disclosures were public from 2017), some short-side analysts. Lesson: for banks, divergence disclosures, concentration to stressed groups and regulator actions on management are disqualifiers; 'cheap' P/B after the first fall is a value trap.

**Lesson:** Divergence = understated NPAs; regulator acting on CEO is a sell signal
**Spotted early by:** RBI asset-quality reviews
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:disqualifiers`, illustrates -> `insight:lender-blowup-signals`, illustrates -> `insight:value-trap-patterns`
**Sources:** <https://www.isas.nus.edu.sg/papers/yes-bank-in-moratorium-how-it-collapsed-and-what-next> ; <https://www.business-standard.com/amp/article/finance/fast-growth-to-quick-fall-the-story-of-yes-bank-s-changing-fortunes-120030501790_1.html> ; <https://www.tickertape.in/blog/yes-bank-crisis/>

`theme:sector-ems-electronics` · confidence: single-source · tickers: DIXON, KAYNES, SYRMA, AMBER, AVALON, PGEL, CYIENTDLM

**How it makes money:** Contract manufacturing; thin conversion margin on pass-through revenue; PLI/ECMS subsidies; component backward integration.

**Metrics that matter:**
- Revenue growth by segment (mobile, consumer, IT hardware, industrial)
- EBITDA margin & absolute EBITDA
- RoCE / asset turns
- Net working capital days
- Top-client share
- PLI income as % of EBITDA
- Domestic value addition %
- Component capex & ECMS approvals

**Value chain and where margins sit:** Global brand (design, IP, demand) -> EMS assembler -> component suppliers (chips, displays, camera modules; mostly imported, highest margins) -> distribution. Brand owners and component makers take most of the profit; assembly is low-margin but scalable.

**Cycle drivers:** Smartphone/consumer electronics demand, brand sourcing shifts, PLI/ECMS policy, tariffs/China+1, component import duties.

**Lead indicators (public India data):**
- MeitY/ICEA electronics production & export data
- Commerce Ministry HS 8517 (telephones) monthly exports
- ECMS approval lists
- Counterpoint/IDC India smartphone shipments
- Client capacity announcements

**What separated winners from losers:** Winners: early policy positioning, capital-light, multi-client, credible component integration, conservative accounting. Losers: one-client dependence, receivables (incl. PLI dues) build-up, RPT/disclosure issues, margin collapse after subsidy roll-off.

**Valuation ranges and peaks/troughs:** P/E 60–120x at 2024–25 peaks for Dixon/Kaynes; EV/EBITDA 40–70x. Pre-PLI (2017–19) Dixon ~30–40x. Value usually sits in EBITDA growth and RoCE, not revenue.

**Current state (Nov 2026):** Dixon Q2 FY27: revenue up strongly (sources give +35% to ₹37,341 cr or +47% to ₹21,794 cr; unreconciled), PBT +9%, PAT ₹411 cr (−45% on lower other income), op margin 2.7% vs 3.8% after mobile PLI ended; ₹1,110 cr PLI receivables outstanding; FY27 ex-Vivo guidance ~₹56,000 cr; display JV commercial production targeted Q4 FY27.

**Classic traps:**
- Capitalising PLI subsidies as permanent margin
- Revenue growth with falling RoCE
- PLI receivables/other income quality
- Single anchor client
- Disclosure/RPT red flags at high multiples

`insight:buffett-mistakes-first-25-years` | confidence: verified | date: 1990-03-02

1989 letter section, Buffett's condensed list of his own errors. (1) Buying control of Berkshire's textile mill because 'the price looked cheap'. The 'cigar butt' approach works only for liquidators: 'never is there just one cockroach in the kitchen' and 'Time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre.' (2) Hochschild Kohn department store, bought below book with real-estate and LIFO 'extras' - 'three years later I was lucky to sell the business for about what I had paid.' Lesson: 'It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Charlie understood this early; I was a slow learner.' (3) 'Good jockeys will do well on good horses, but not on broken-down nags'; 'when a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for bad economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact' (first said in 1980s letters, repeated 1985 with the leaking-boat line: 'energy devoted to changing vessels is likely to be more productive than energy devoted to patching leaks'). (4) 'Easy does it': 'we concentrated on identifying one-foot hurdles that we could step over'; 'we've done better by avoiding dragons than by slaying them.' Exception: 'a marvelous business encounters a one-time huge, but solvable, problem' (AmEx, GEICO). (5) Errors of omission: passing on big purchases he understood - 'the cost of this thumb-sucking has been huge.' Related 1979 line: 'turnarounds seldom turn'. Actionable: a cheap price on a structurally poor Indian business (commodity textiles, sub-scale PSU, leveraged infra) is not a margin of safety; time compounds against you.

Sources:
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1989.html
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1985.html
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1979.html

body:
`size = min(kelly_fraction × f*, tier cap at cost, liquidity cap)`, then 0 if any gate blocks.
- `f*` maximises `E[ln(1 + f·(M/H − 1))]` over the scenario outcomes, after v1.2 tail anchoring (the raw-model f* is shown alongside) (each spread by 5-point Gauss-Hermite on σ, with the blow-up as a point mass). `H` is the index hurdle multiple, so the bet is measured against the alternative.
- Kelly fraction defaults to 0.25 (`strategy:thorp-kelly`).
- Tier caps (`strategy:position-sizing`): core 5%, satellite 4%, speculative 2%.
- Liquidity cap = `adv_pct × ADV × days_to_exit ÷ portfolio value`, in the same money units.
- Phase A: every size is a **paper size**. In practice mode the card says that this is a mechanical rule output, not a size for anyone.
